summary: The machine has the tools and DocumentDB MCP/data-plane skills required to build the Node.js + Mongoose store-locator sample against the provided live Azure DocumentDB M30 cluster. Key agent skills (indexing, driver/connection guidance, local gateway docs, vector & full-text search, monitoring) and the 'documentdb' MCP server are present so the code, index creation, seeding and verification steps can run. Several cold answers in the prompt review mix up Azure Cosmos DB (RU-based Mongo API) and the vCore-managed product now named Azure DocumentDB; those confusions are corrected and documented below. Missing optional developer accelerators (DocumentDB Agent Kit) and a few convenience CLI tools (mongosh) would speed manual debugging but are not blocking.
summary_points: All essential runtime and agent tools for the sample are available: Node (v24), npx, npm, Docker, git, the 'documentdb' MCP server and the Microsoft Learn (learn) MCP server.
Installed documentdb-* skills cover schema, indexing, connection and local-deployment guidance needed to implement the sample and verify it against the live cluster.

Several cold answers wrongly described Cosmos DB (RU/ databaseAccounts / port 10255) instead of Azure DocumentDB's vCore mongoClusters resource model — these are corrected with Learn articles and the documentdb skill docs.
Missing but non-blocking items: DocumentDB Agent Kit accelerator (would speed development) and mongosh (handy for ad-hoc checks); guidance/workarounds are provided.

Because the inventory and authoritative docs verify the product surfaces the builder needs, the build can start; some facts must be used as corrected in this report (resource type, provisioning CLI group, connection-string form, billing model, vector/index syntax, Entra-auth details).

tools.name: node
tools.needed_for: Run and build the Node.js + Mongoose sample (npm, npx), run tests and start the Express server.
tools.workaround: Install Node 24 (nvm or installer) on the machine.

tools.name: npx / npm
tools.needed_for: Install dependencies, run scripts, and optionally install agent skills via npx.
tools.impact_if_missing: Can't install packages or start dev scripts.

tools.name: git
tools.needed_for: Source control for the sample repo and to fetch sample assets or agent skills (if needed).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to manage repo; could still copy files manually.
tools.workaround: Use zipped sources or GitHub web UI to download samples.

tools.name: docker
tools.needed_for: Optional: run the local DocumentDB gateway container for offline integration tests or reproducible local dev (gateway image runs Mongo protocol on port 10260).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run local gateway container for isolated integration tests; still can run against live cluster.
tools.workaround: Test against the live DocumentDB cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI) as required by the run environment.

tools.name: az (Azure CLI)
tools.needed_for: Inspect Azure resources if needed (read-only); useful for retrieving connection strings or role assignments during verification.
tools.detail: az CLI installed (2.89.1) with cosmosdb-preview/documentd extension visible in inventory detail.
tools.impact_if_missing: Less convenient to inspect resource group or cluster metadata from CLI; still possible via MCP servers or portal.
tools.workaround: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server to list resources and the Azure Portal.

tools.name: mongosh
tools.needed_for: Convenient manual checks of connectivity, indexes and ad-hoc queries against the cluster (handy while developing).
tools.impact_if_missing: Cannot run a local mongosh shell for quick manual debugging; however the 'documentdb' MCP server provides data-plane tools for inspecting collections, indexes, sample docs and running aggregation/explain.
tools.workaround: Use the 'documentdb' MCP server tools (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_aggregate, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation) to inspect data and run aggregation plans.

tools.name: documentdb MCP server (data-plane)
tools.needed_for: Create collections and indexes, insert sample data, run aggregations (including $geoNear), and explain plans against the live Azure DocumentDB cluster. The build instructions require verifying created objects against this server.
tools.detail: documentdb MCP server present and available with 18 read-only tools (list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain_operation, etc.).
tools.impact_if_missing: Would lose ability to programmatically verify indexes, run explain or sample documents from within the agent harness; would need mongosh or Azure portal.
tools.workaround: Use mongosh (if installed) or the Azure portal to inspect the cluster; but documentdb MCP is the best verification tool and is available.

tools.name: learn (Microsoft Learn MCP server)
tools.needed_for: Ground facts in authoritative Microsoft Learn docs (index shapes, CLI groups, resource types, connection-string formats, geospatial units, vector index syntax, OIDC auth details).
tools.detail: learn MCP server present with documentation search and fetch tools.
tools.impact_if_missing: Agent couldn't verify product facts against Microsoft Learn pages; higher risk of confusion with neighbours.
tools.workaround: Rely on bundled agent skills' documentation, but the Learn server is available and was used for grounding.

tools.name: Installed documentdb-* agent skills
tools.needed_for: Authoritative, domain-specific guidance while implementing the sample: schema & indexing (documentdb-indexing), driver best practices (documentdb-driver), connection tuning (documentdb-connection), local dev (documentdb-local-deployment), security/Entra guidance (documentdb-security), vector and search patterns (documentdb-vector-search, documentdb-full-text-search), and deployment helper docs (documentdb-azure-deployment).
tools.impact_if_missing: Harder to produce best-practice code and index shapes; more risk of subtle runtime misconfiguration.
tools.workaround: Rely on Microsoft Learn docs; however the installed skills are present and recommended.

tools.name: azd / bicep / terraform
tools.needed_for: Not required by this sample (the run environment forbids provisioning another cluster); useful only if the builder wanted to provision infrastructure.
tools.detail: azd, bicep and terraform not found on PATH per inventory.
tools.impact_if_missing: No impact for this sample; provisioning another cluster is disallowed by run policy.
tools.workaround: Use the existing cluster and the documentdb MCP server. If provisioning is needed, install bicep/azd/terraform per official docs.

accelerators_missed: DocumentDB Agent Kit (npx skills add Azure/documentdb-agent-kit) - would bundle example repos and quickstart scaffolding that speeds building this sample.

confusions.question: What is the Azure resource provider namespace and resource type of an Azure DocumentDB cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Provider namespace: Microsoft.DocumentDB. Primary resource type: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the Cosmos DB / DocumentDB account resource).
confusions.grounded_answer: The vCore-managed DocumentDB cluster resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not the databaseAccounts resource).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn (templates) - Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (deployment-language-bicep)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Shared provider namespace 'Microsoft.DocumentDB' and historical naming: older Cosmos DB account resources (databaseAccounts) are for the RU-based Cosmos Mongo API, so a quick memory lookup can return databaseAccounts instead of the newer mongoClusters resource type for vCore clusters.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempted to deploy or reference Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (instead of Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters) they would be targeting the RU-based Cosmos DB account resource; ARM/Bicep/Terraform templates and CLI calls would be incorrect for vCore clusters and the builder might fail to find or create the intended resource.
improvements: Update quickstart and sample templates to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore clusters and explicitly note the distinction from Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts (the RU Cosmos DB account).
Add a short deprecation/clarification note on the top of any docs that still show databaseAccounts for MongoDB use to point readers to mongoClusters when they intend vCore clusters.

confusions.question: Which Azure CLI command group creates and manages a cluster? Is it in the core CLI or an extension?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the built-in az cosmosdb command group in the core Azure CLI. Example create command: az cosmosdb create --name myDocDbAccount --resource-group myRg --kind MongoDB ...
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed DocumentDB clusters the relevant CLI commands are 'az documentdb mongocluster' (also surfaced under az cosmosdb mongocluster in some docs/CLI versions); the create/list connection-string commands are provided via the documentdb/ cosmosdb CLI command groups (some commands live in preview extensions).
confusions.grounding_source: Azure CLI docs for 'az documentdb mongocluster' and 'az cosmosdb mongocluster' (Microsoft Learn)

grounding_links.title: az documentdb mongocluster (Azure CLI docs)
az cosmosdb mongocluster create (Azure CLI docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Cosmos DB and DocumentDB functionality historically shared CLI groups; newer vCore cluster commands are exposed under 'documentdb' or 'cosmosdb' extensions in recent az CLI releases, and older memory recalled the generic az cosmosdb create pattern (which targets databaseAccounts).

confusion_sources.title: az cosmosdb create (core CLI) - creates Cosmos DB account (databaseAccounts)

confusions.build_risk: Using az cosmosdb create (databaseAccounts) would create or target the RU-based Cosmos DB account resource and not the vCore mongoClusters; the wrong CLI group will lead to provisioning/management failures for the intended cluster type.
improvements: Clarify in the Azure CLI quickstarts and samples the exact command group to use for vCore DocumentDB clusters (az documentdb mongocluster or az cosmosdb mongocluster) and call out whether the command is in a preview/extension.
Add a note in the 'az cosmosdb' docs that points to 'az documentdb' commands for vCore workloads so agents don't conflate the two.

confusions.question: Which Bicep and Terraform resource types deploy a cluster?
confusions.cold_answer: Bicep: Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts@2021-04-15 ... Terraform: azurerm_cosmosdb_account
confusions.grounded_answer: For vCore-managed clusters the correct Bicep/ARM/Terraform resource type is Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (or the corresponding azapi/avm module for mongo-cluster); azurerm_cosmosdb_account / Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts is for RU-based Cosmos DB accounts, not vCore DocumentDB clusters.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn templates: Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters

grounding_links.title: Microsoft.DocumentDB mongoClusters (ARM / Bicep / Terraform examples)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older Cosmos DB Mongo API used databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account; vCore clusters are a newer resource type (mongoClusters). The shared provider namespace and historical naming cause the mix-up.
confusions.build_risk: Using the databaseAccounts/azurerm_cosmosdb_account resource type will not create the intended vCore mongo cluster; deployment templates would target the wrong product and fail validation or produce a mismatched resource.
improvements: Update sample IaC templates and the agent kit templates to use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters for vCore clusters and include one-liner guidance that azurerm_cosmosdb_account is for RU-based Cosmos accounts.

confusions.question: What does a connection string look like: scheme, host suffix, port, and the options it must carry?
confusions.cold_answer: Typical Azure Cosmos DB Mongo API mongodb://<user>:<pwd>@<account>.mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255/?ssl=true&replicaSet=globaldb&retryWrites=false&appName=@<account>@
confusions.grounded_answer: There are two distinct connection-string families in the docs: (1) RU-based Azure Cosmos DB Mongo API accounts typically use host suffix *.mongo.cosmos.azure.com and port 10255 with options like ssl=true, replicaSet=globaldb, retryWrites=false; (2) vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB mongoClusters expose cluster-specific connection strings (the CLI/portal/az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings or ARM outputs) and commonly support mongodb+srv forms and MONGODB-OIDC settings for Entra-auth. Use the connection string provided by the cluster (DOCUMENTDB_URI in the run environment).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: 'Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB' (10255 examples) and 'mongoClusters' connection-string docs (use listConnectionStrings for vCore clusters)

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (connection string, port 10255)
az documentdb mongocluster list-connection-strings / MongoClusters SDK docs

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The older RU-based Cosmos DB Mongo API uses the well-known mongo.cosmos.azure.com:10255 pattern; vCore DocumentDB mongoClusters are surfaced differently and may publish SRV records or cluster-style connection strings. The memory recalled the Cosmos pattern rather than the vCore cluster pattern.

confusion_sources.title: Cosmos DB MongoDB connection string examples (10255)

confusions.build_risk: Using the Cosmos (10255) connection-string pattern against a vCore DocumentDB cluster may fail to connect or misuse required auth/query options; the sample must read the provided DOCUMENTDB_URI (per run environment) and pass it unchanged to mongoose/MongoClient.
improvements: In all Node/README samples, instruct builders to read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env and not to hard-code connection string patterns; show both common patterns (10255/cosmos-host and mongoClusters SRV) and explain which one applies.

confusions.question: How is capacity provisioned and billed: request units, compute tiers with vCores, serverless, or something else?
confusions.cold_answer: Capacity is billed as RU/s (Request Units) or serverless in the managed Cosmos-style service. vCore-based billing is not the standard model for the MongoDB API.
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB (vCore-managed clusters) capacity is provisioned as compute tiers (vCore/sku such as M30) + storage (vCore model). The RU-based model applies to the RU Cosmos DB accounts (Cosmos DB / Mongo API RU throughput).
confusions.grounding_source: Azure DocumentDB overview and at-a-glance / compare docs for vCore vs RU Cosmos DB

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (overview & naming) - vCore model
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (pricing model: compute vCores + storage)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The MongoDB API exists in two forms in Azure: RU-based Cosmos accounts (historical Cosmos Mongo API) and vCore-based DocumentDB clusters (newer). The cold answer described the RU model while the run environment and sample target a vCore cluster (M30).
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumed RU-based pricing/throughput they might attempt to set RU throughput parameters in code or IaC for a vCore cluster and fail to configure or size the cluster correctly.
improvements: Add an explicit statement in the quickstarts and agent kit that vCore DocumentDB clusters use compute (vCore) SKUs (e.g., M30) and are not provisioned via RU/s.
Add a short comparison table (vCore vs RU) to the 'getting started' doc for agents to consult.

confusions.question: Which authentication methods are supported, and how does a driver authenticate with Microsoft Entra ID?
confusions.cold_answer: Primary auth is username/password (SCRAM) and AAD is possible by obtaining an OAuth2 access token and supplying it (authSource="$external" and authMechanism=PLAIN/X509-style integration).
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports both native SCRAM credentials and Microsoft Entra ID (OIDC) data-plane authentication for clusters. The driver-level integration uses the MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism and connection-string properties such as authMechanism=MONGODB-OIDC and authMechanismProperties=ENVIRONMENT:azure,TOKEN_RESOURCE:..., or the mongodb+srv form; the provider docs show how to supply client-id or managed identity and how to use MONGODB-OIDC or OIDC flows in clients and tools.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID (MONGODB-OIDC examples)

grounding_links.title: Connect to Azure DocumentDB using role-based access control and Microsoft Entra ID

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described a generic OAuth2/token-as-password approach and an 'external auth' pattern rather than the documented MONGODB-OIDC mechanism and connection-string properties recommended by Azure DocumentDB docs.

confusion_sources.title: Docs showing SCRAM and role-based access control (RBAC) for Cosmos DB (older pages)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder attempts to implement Entra auth by passing an OAuth token as a normal password with authSource='$external' they will use the wrong auth mechanism and connections will fail. Use the documented MONGODB-OIDC connection-string parameters or the portal-provided connection strings.
improvements: Document the precise connection-string parameters and example code snippets for common driver platforms (Node.js, mongosh, MongoDB Compass) that show MONGODB-OIDC usage and managed-identity examples.

confusions.question: Which client library should an application use? Is there a service-specific SDK?
confusions.cold_answer: Use standard MongoDB drivers (mongodb, Mongoose). There is no separate service-specific MongoDB driver.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use the official MongoDB drivers (Node.js mongodb driver and Mongoose for ODM). For management/provisioning use Azure CLI / ARM / az documentdb etc., but the data-plane app should use standard MongoDB drivers.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB and Node.js Mongoose tutorials

grounding_links.title: Connect a MongoDB application to Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB
Tutorial: Use Mongoose with Azure DocumentDB

confusions.question: Which vector index types are supported, and what does the command that creates one look like?
confusions.cold_answer: Create a knnVector index with db.myCollection.createIndex({ embedding: 'knnVector' }, { knnVector: { dimensions: 1536, metric: 'cosine', method: 'hnsw' } })
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports vector index kinds 'vector-ivf', 'vector-hnsw' and 'vector-diskann' and you create them via the 'createIndexes' database command with a 'cosmosSearch' key and a 'cosmosSearchOptions' (or 'kind' field) describing dimensions, similarity metric and method. The public docs provide the exact createIndexes JSON templates (cosmosSearchOptions.kind = 'vector-hnsw' | 'vector-ivf' | 'vector-diskann').
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB (vector-search docs, createIndexes templates)

grounding_links.title: Integrated vector store in Azure DocumentDB - createIndexes templates and vector kinds
Quickstart: Use vector search with Node.js in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer used a MongoDB Atlas/knnVector-style syntax which differs from Azure DocumentDB's createIndexes/cosmosSearchOptions JSON format and the 'vector-ivf/vector-hnsw/vector-diskann' kinds.

confusion_sources.title: Example Atlas knnVector docs (typical third-party syntax)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder used the Atlas-style createIndex call, index creation would fail. Use the documentdb createIndexes templates (cosmosSearch/cosmosSearchOptions) documented in the vector-search docs.
improvements: Provide a short 'create vector index' code snippet for Node.js in the agent kit and quickstarts using createIndexes + cosmosSearchOptions to reduce copying of Atlas syntax.

confusions.question: How are full-text search and hybrid search done?
confusions.cold_answer: Integrate with Azure Cognitive Search or use the service's built-in text indexing; hybrid is done by combining vector results and text results in application code or external search service.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB provides a built-in full-text (BM25) engine created with createSearchIndexes and queried with $search aggregation stage; hybrid search (BM25 + vector) is supported natively and DocumentDB recommends server-side Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF) or pipeline approaches to combine BM25 and vector results. Using Azure Cognitive Search is unnecessary and adds complexity; prefer the built-in createSearchIndexes + $search hybrid approach when available.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB and Hybrid search docs

grounding_links.title: Full-text search in Azure DocumentDB (createSearchIndexes & $search)
Hybrid search (BM25 + vector) and Reciprocal Rank Fusion

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Memory suggested using Azure Cognitive Search as an integration option (valid historically) but DocumentDB now ships an integrated BM25 search index and native hybrid search primitives that the sample should prefer for simplicity and performance.

confusion_sources.title: Azure Cognitive Search integration patterns (older guidance)

confusions.build_risk: If the builder wired in Azure Cognitive Search rather than using createSearchIndexes they would add unnecessary infrastructure and complexity and miss the native hybrid search primitives documented for DocumentDB.
improvements: Document the recommended route (createSearchIndexes + $search + RRF) clearly in the agent-kit search guidance and discourage routine use of external search services unless there's a specific reason.

confusions.question: Which MongoDB wire protocol or server versions are supported, and which commonly used MongoDB features are not?
confusions.cold_answer: Supported versions vary; examples include 4.0, 4.2, 5.0 and — in newer clusters — 7.0. Some advanced admin commands or server-side JS may be limited.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB supports modern MongoDB wire protocol versions (examples shown in docs include 5.0, 6.0, 7.0 and newer), and the mongoClusters resource has a serverVersion parameter defaulting to the latest available; feature-level compatibility is documented per serverVersion. Some admin commands and special internal server-state commands are not exposed in this managed service. Check the compatibility matrix for per-version operator/stage support.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: MongoDB Query Language compatibility and 'serverVersion' property on mongoClusters docs

grounding_links.title: MongoDB Query Language (MQL) compatibility in Azure DocumentDB
MongoClusterProperties (serverVersion) and supported server versions

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer listed example versions but didn't highlight that vCore clusters expose a serverVersion parameter and that compatibility is versioned and documented per-version; memory produced a generic list rather than citing the documented compatibility matrix.
confusions.build_risk: Assuming a certain server-version feature (for example a stage introduced in a later MongoDB release) without verifying the cluster’s serverVersion could cause runtime errors.
improvements: Encourage samples to read the cluster's serverVersion (via portal/az or the documentdb MCP server) and confirm required operators against the compatibility matrix before using them.

confusions.question: How do you run the database locally for development and tests: which image or emulator, and which port?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the Azure Cosmos DB Emulator (Windows or Linux Docker) which exposes the MongoDB-compatible endpoint on port 10255 (or mapped port).
confusions.grounded_answer: For Azure DocumentDB local development the recommended Gateway Docker image is ghcr.io/documentdb/documentdb/documentdb-local (gateway) and it exposes the MongoDB protocol on port 10260 (and PostgreSQL on 9712). The DocumentDB local gateway is the recommended local dev image for this service; the Cosmos DB emulator is distinct and applies to Cosmos DB accounts, not vCore DocumentDB gateway parity.
confusions.grounding_source: documentdb-local-deployment skill resources (local gateway image and port 10260)

grounding_links.title: documentdb-local-deployment
Local gateway image & ports (docs)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer conflated the Cosmos DB Emulator (which targets Cosmos DB accounts) and the DocumentDB local gateway image used for vCore DocumentDB development. Both are local dev options but they differ in image and default ports.
confusions.build_risk: Trying to run the Cosmos DB emulator (or expecting 10255) instead of the DocumentDB gateway (10260) will make the local dev instance not match the intended cluster configuration; the sample run-environment requires using the live cluster but the local gateway instructions in the skill should be followed if the builder chooses to run a local container.
improvements: Add an explicit 'local dev vs emulator' note to the quickstart README that states: use the DocumentDB gateway image (port 10260) for DocumentDB vCore local parity and the Cosmos DB emulator only for Cosmos (RU) accounts.

confusions.question: Are change streams supported, and does anything have to be enabled first?
confusions.cold_answer: Change streams are supported on managed clusters that expose a sufficiently recent MongoDB API version (3.6+). No per-collection flag is normally required.
confusions.grounded_answer: Change streams are supported. For single-shard clusters standard change streams work. For multishard clusters, Azure DocumentDB supports multi-shard change streams in preview and you must enable the 'Change streams for multishard clusters' feature from the cluster Features page and observe prerequisites (Rebalancer off). Resume tokens and startAtOperationTime are supported; docs describe how to enable and use multi-shard change streams.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB (feature enablement and multi-shard preview)

grounding_links.title: Change streams in Azure DocumentDB

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer omitted the multishard enablement detail; in the managed DocumentDB product there is an explicit feature toggle and prerequisites for cluster-wide (multi-shard) change streams.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes multi-shard change streams are on by default they may attempt to open a cluster-wide stream and fail; check cluster Features and enable multi-shard change streams if the sample intends to exercise that capability.
improvements: Add a confirmation step in the sample README: ‘If you need multi-shard change streams enable the cluster feature: Features > Change streams for multishard clusters’ and link to the portal steps.

confusions.question: Which MCP server gives an agent data-plane tools for this service? Does the general Azure MCP Server cover it?
confusions.cold_answer: Use the documentdb MCP server. The general Azure MCP server does not replace service-specific tooling.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct: the documentdb MCP server provides the data-plane tools (list_databases, create_index, aggregate, explain_operation, etc.). The azure MCP server is complementary for control-plane tasks; data-plane inspection should use the documentdb MCP server.
confusions.grounding_source: Machine inventory (documentdb MCP server listed) and MCP tool descriptions

grounding_links.title: documentdb MCP server (inventory)

confusions.question: What was this service called before, and how does it relate to Azure Cosmos DB and to the open-source DocumentDB project?
confusions.cold_answer: Historically Microsoft marketed a service called DocumentDB which evolved into Azure Cosmos DB. The name 'DocumentDB' is legacy; Azure Cosmos DB is the broader managed service. The open-source 'DocumentDB' project name has been used elsewhere.
confusions.grounded_answer: This requires nuance: the product now called Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility) was previously named 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)' and was rebranded in late 2025/2026 to Azure DocumentDB. It is a distinct offering from the RU-based Azure Cosmos DB (databaseAccounts) and is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine. Also note that the original Azure DocumentDB (2014-2017) became Azure Cosmos DB historically — the name overlaps are a common source of confusion.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: FAQ and 'at-a-glance' pages that document renaming and relationship to Cosmos DB and the open-source DocumentDB project

grounding_links.title: Azure DocumentDB FAQ - how it relates to Azure Cosmos DB
What is Azure DocumentDB (overview & naming)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: Multiple rebrands and similarly named products (old DocumentDB -> Cosmos DB; vCore Cosmos DB for MongoDB -> Azure DocumentDB) cause memory mismatches.
confusions.build_risk: Public-facing sample text that uses the wrong product name may mislead users; CLI and template commands may target the wrong resource type if the wrong name is used.
improvements: Add an explicit 'naming and mapping' FAQ page in the agent kit that maps 'Azure DocumentDB', 'Azure Cosmos DB for MongoDB (vCore)', and 'Azure Cosmos DB (RU)' to their resource types and intended use-cases.

confusions.question: What engine is underneath, and does that change anything in application code?
confusions.cold_answer: Underneath is the Cosmos-style managed engine with a MongoDB compatibility layer; for application code you generally use the normal MongoDB drivers but expect some behavioral differences.
confusions.grounded_answer: Azure DocumentDB is built on the open-source DocumentDB engine (DocumentDB project) that Microsoft publishes; that engine implements the MongoDB wire protocol for compatibility. For application code you use normal MongoDB drivers (Mongoose), but there are service-specific differences and recommended connection options (tls, driver options) and some admin commands are not exposed. The underlying engine is DocumentDB (open-source) rather than the Cosmos DB RU-engine.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn: 'What is Azure DocumentDB' and 'At a glance' pages describing the DocumentDB engine (open-source) and compatibility

grounding_links.title: What is Azure DocumentDB (with MongoDB compatibility)?
Azure DocumentDB at a glance (engine & implementation)

confusions.why_the_confusion_arose: The cold answer described a generic 'Cosmos-style' engine; in fact Azure DocumentDB runs on the open-source DocumentDB engine (distinct from Cosmos DB's RU engine) which affects certain capabilities and the project's local/gateway images.
confusions.build_risk: If the builder assumes a Cosmos DB RU engine they might reach for RU-specific features or configuration and run into incompatible behavior.
improvements: State the engine explicitly in the agent kit landing page and in sample READMEs: 'Azure DocumentDB runs on DocumentDB (open-source) and supports MongoDB drivers; compare to Cosmos (RU) where noted.'

confusions.question: What database name will the sample use?
confusions.cold_answer: The sample will use the database named sample_retail_20 for all created collections and indexes.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — the run environment and sample prompt require using database 'sample_retail_20'.
confusions.grounding_source: Sample prompt and run-environment guidance

confusions.question: What collection schema and index does this sample need for geospatial search?
confusions.cold_answer: Collection: stores. GeoJSON Point with { type: 'Point', coordinates: [lon, lat] } and create 2dsphere index on location.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — use GeoJSON Point with coordinates ordered [longitude, latitude] and create a 2dsphere index (db.stores.createIndex({ location: '2dsphere' })).
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn geospatial docs and documentdb-indexing skill guidance

grounding_links.title: Geospatial support and $geoNear docs

confusions.question: What aggregation stage does the /nearby endpoint need to run to find stores by radius?
confusions.cold_answer: Use $geoNear aggregation as the pipeline's first stage with near, distanceField, maxDistance (meters), spherical:true.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — $geoNear should be the first stage; maxDistance is expressed in meters and spherical:true is required for 2dsphere indexes. Also the $geoNear stage requires the 'key' option in some DocumentDB variants; verify with the cluster if needed.
confusions.grounding_source: Microsoft Learn $geoNear and geospatial operator docs

grounding_links.title: $geoNear documentation (distance units in meters)

confusions.question: How should the app read the connection string and connect with Mongoose in code?
confusions.cold_answer: Read DOCUMENTDB_URI from env and connect with mongoose.connect(process.env.DOCUMENTDB_URI, { useNewUrlParser: true, useUnifiedTopology: true, tls: true }).
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct — read the connection URI from DOCUMENTDB_URI and pass it to mongoose/MongoClient; include recommended driver options and do not log or write the secret. Use the exact options required by the portal-provided connection string if present (e.g. appName, retryWrites, replicaSet) and allow TLS. Follow documentdb-driver and documentdb-connection skill recommendations for pool and timeout tuning.

confusions.question: Which Node and Mongoose versions should the sample target and how to declare them?
confusions.cold_answer: Target Node.js 24 and mongoose 7.x, declare in package.json with ^7.0.0.
confusions.grounded_answer: Correct as a reasonable default: Node 24 (the run environment has v24) and Mongoose 7.x are compatible; declare dependencies in package.json and include start scripts. The documentdb-driver and local-deployment skills recommend latest stable mongoose 7.x for Node 24.

information_gaps.title: API surface choices for /nearby endpoint
information_gaps.description: The prompt did not specify whether /nearby should accept lat/lon/radius as query parameters or JSON body, nor naming conventions (lat/lng or lat/lon) or error-handling behaviors. I checked the prompt review and docs; this is an API design choice and not specified by any skill or Learn page. The builder must pick a convention (recommend: query params ?lat=&lon=&radiusMeters=) and document it in README.

information_gaps.title: Seed dataset content and licensing
information_gaps.description: The prompt leaves unspecified what sample dataset to include (size, realistic coordinates, stock model). Documentdb-local-deployment skill shows how to seed data but does not supply a canonical example dataset or license. The builder should create a small synthetic idempotent seed (10–20 stores) and include it in the repo; the decision isn't answered by any skill.

information_gaps.title: Definition of done / acceptance tests
information_gaps.description: No single authoritative source states exact acceptance criteria for this sample (number of returned results, sorting tolerances, edge cases). The builder must choose reasonable criteria (e.g., /nearby returns stores sorted by distance, distance includes returned distance field in meters, opens/closes filter works) and document test steps.

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Use Microsoft.DocumentDB/mongoClusters (not Microsoft.DocumentDB/databaseAccounts) when referencing or describing the vCore-managed Azure DocumentDB resource; deploy IaC and check cluster metadata accordingly.

Read the provided DOCUMENTDB_URI environment variable at runtime and pass it unchanged to mongoose.connect / MongoClient; do not hard-code connection-string patterns (the cluster publishes the correct form).

guidance_for_builder.instruction: Create your geospatial index with a 2dsphere index on the GeoJSON Point field and use $geoNear as the first aggregation stage; maxDistance and returned distances are in meters.

If you plan to use Microsoft Entra ID for data-plane auth, use the documented MONGODB-OIDC authMechanism and the connection-string parameters shown in the 'Connect using Microsoft Entra ID' doc rather than trying to pass a raw OAuth token as the password with authSource='$external'.

inventory_recommendations.name: azd
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this sample because no new resources will be provisioned; leave absent. If provisioning is later required, install the Azure Developer CLI (azd) per Microsoft Learn.

inventory_recommendations.name: bicep
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not needed for this sample since the run environment forbids creating a new cluster. If the agent kit later generates Bicep for users, document using 'az bicep build' when bicep is absent or include az bicep in CI images.

inventory_recommendations.name: terraform
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Not required for this build run (no provisioning). If IaC authors want Terraform support, provide Terraform module examples in the agent kit rather than requiring terraform on every developer machine.

inventory_recommendations.name: dotnet
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: The sample is Node.js; dotnet is optional unless the builder wants to run .NET samples or Azure Functions triggers locally. If needed, instruct how to install dotnet in the README.

inventory_recommendations.name: mongosh
inventory_recommendations.recommendation: Useful for interactive debugging and ad-hoc verification of collections/indexes; install mongosh (MongoDB Shell) on the dev machine or use Docker client images. Workaround: the documentdb MCP server provides equivalent data-plane commands (documentdb_find_documents, documentdb_aggregate, documentdb_list_indexes, documentdb_explain_operation) that the agent should use if mongosh is absent.
